title: Feds Offer Lodging and Food as Iowa Prepares for Massive Lead Explosives Blast
snippet: Federal agencies are providing emergency housing, meals, and evacuation aid to Iowa residents ahead of a controversial military detonation involving nearly five tons of volatile lead azide.
content:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — Federal authorities are offering emergency lodging, meal assistance, and free transportation to residents in southeastern Iowa as crews prepare for a high-stakes controlled explosion of nearly five tons of degraded military explosives on Wednesday morning.

The planned detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown follows days of delays, public backlash, legal friction, and high-level government intervention over potential environmental and public health risks associated with airborne lead fallout. Defense models indicate airborne lead dust from the blast could drift up to 100 miles southwest, potentially crossing into neighboring Missouri.

Evacuation and Emergency Relocation Assistance

The U.S. Army and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) are urging residents living within a five-mile zone southwest of the facility to evacuate ahead of the 9:00 a.m. detonation. Officials emphasized that pregnant individuals, young children, and people with pre-existing respiratory conditions face the highest risk from potential dust exposure.

FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton stated that federal agencies were instructed by the White House to 'spare no expense' to keep surrounding communities safe. The government has established a hotline (1-800-621-3362) and is covering short-term lodging, food, and transit costs for displaced residents through Friday.

Enhanced Blast Mitigations Put in Place

Addressing mounting public concern, military leaders revealed extensive mitigation measures added to the blast zone over recent days. The containment design includes massive sand barriers around the explosive site, two reinforced walls consisting of eight 16,000-gallon water tanks, and high-expansion aqueous foam meant to absorb particulates generated by the blast.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle defended the decision to proceed, calling the controlled blast the only viable option to prevent a catastrophic, spontaneous explosion. The nearly 10,000-pound stockpile of aging lead azide, a primary explosive phased out years ago, has degraded to a point where routine liquid maintenance can no longer be safely performed.

State Disaster Declarations and Widespread Testing

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for Des Moines, Lee, and Van Buren counties, mobilizing state resources and authorizing up to 100 Iowa National Guard members to assist with public safety and door-to-door notifications. Emergency response agencies in Missouri and Illinois have also been placed on alert.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has deployed more than 150 field teams and four mobile testing laboratories across three states to monitor air, soil, and water quality before and after the blast. Additionally, the U.S. Department of Agriculture is coordinating with roughly 350 local farms to help livestock producers shelter animals and protect regional agricultural assets.
